title: C++ vectors: growth, iterators and safe erasing

authoring.author: Parikshaa content team
authoring.originality: Written for Parikshaa: our own lesson text and examples on c++ vectors: growth, iterators and safe erasing, examples, code, quiz and explanations; no text from any site, book or course.

outcomes: can explain size, capacity and why push_back is amortised O(1)
can say which vector operations invalidate iterators and references
can remove elements correctly with the erase-remove idiom

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.body: `std::vector` is the container you will use in nearly every C++ solution, in contests and in interviews. It is fast because its elements sit next to each other in memory, and that same fact causes its two famous traps: references that suddenly point to freed memory, and loops that skip elements while erasing. Both appear in "find the bug" rounds.

sections.heading: Size, capacity and reallocation
sections.body:
A vector owns one block of memory. **`size()`** is how many elements are in use; **`capacity()`** is how many fit before the block is full.

When `push_back` finds the block full, the vector **reallocates**: it gets a bigger block (libstdc++, the library with g++, doubles it), moves every element across, and frees the old block. One push can therefore cost `O(n)`. But because capacity doubles, a long run of pushes copies each element only a few times on average, so `push_back` is **amortised `O(1)`**.

If you know the final size, call **`reserve(n)`** first: one allocation, no reallocation during the loop.

> **Note:** Doubling means the total copying for `n` pushes is at most about `1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n < 2n` element moves. That geometric sum is the whole proof of amortised `O(1)`, and interviewers like to hear it.

sections.heading: Watching capacity grow
sections.body: The program prints each time the capacity changes while pushing 1 to 17, then the same with `reserve(17)`.

code.expected_output:
size 1 -> capacity 1
size 2 -> capacity 2
size 3 -> capacity 4
size 5 -> capacity 8
size 9 -> capacity 16
size 17 -> capacity 32
with reserve(17): capacity 17
code.caption: A vector grows by reallocating; reserve avoids it

sections.heading: Iterator and reference invalidation
sections.body:
An iterator, a pointer or a reference into a vector refers to a place in its memory block. Two kinds of operation break them:

- **Reallocation** (a `push_back`, `insert` or `resize` that exceeds capacity): the whole block moves, so **every** iterator, pointer and reference into the vector becomes invalid.
- **`erase` and `insert` without reallocation**: elements after the position shift, so iterators, pointers and references **at or after** that position are invalid; earlier ones stay valid.

Using an invalid iterator is undefined behaviour: often it seems to work, then crashes in a test you did not run.

Erasing inside a loop has a second, quieter problem. After `erase(begin() + i)` the next element **slides into position `i`**, and the loop's `i++` jumps over it. Two absent marks in a row means one survives.

sections.heading: Erasing the wrong way and the right way
sections.body: Both versions try to remove every `-1` (an absent mark). The index loop leaves one behind; the **erase-remove idiom** removes all of them in one pass.

code.caption: Erasing inside an index loop skips elements; erase-remove does not

sections.heading: How erase-remove works
sections.body:
`std::remove(first, last, value)` does **not** remove anything from the container: it cannot, because it only has iterators. It walks the range once and **moves every element it keeps to the front**, in order, then returns an iterator to the new logical end. The elements after that point are left over and unspecified.

`v.erase(newEnd, v.end())` then actually shrinks the vector. Together they take one linear pass, `O(n)`, compared with `O(n^2)` for erasing elements one by one (each `erase` shifts the rest).

Trace it on `70 -1 -1 85 -1 90`: kept elements 70, 85, 90 are moved to the front, `remove` returns an iterator to position 3, and `erase` cuts the last three slots. Since C++20 there is `std::erase(v, value)` that does both steps, but many judges still compile as C++17, so learn the idiom.

For a condition instead of a value, use `remove_if` with a lambda: `v.erase(remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int m) { return m < 0; }), v.end());`.

If you really must erase inside a loop, use the iterator that `erase` returns: `it = v.erase(it);` and only `++it` when you did not erase. That keeps the iterator valid and does not skip, though it is still `O(n^2)` in the worst case.

sections.heading: Common mix-ups
sections.body:
**Many students think `remove` shrinks the vector.** It only reorders and returns the new end; `size()` is unchanged until you call `erase`.

**Many students think `reserve(n)` creates n elements.** It only allocates capacity; `size()` is still 0, and `v[0]` is out of bounds. `resize(n)` creates elements.

**Many students think a reference into a vector stays valid as long as the vector exists.** Any reallocation invalidates it, even if you only pushed at the end.

sections.heading: Interview questions
sections.body: Answers as a strong candidate would say them.

qa.q: Why is push_back amortised O(1) if it sometimes copies everything?
qa.a: Capacity grows geometrically, typically doubling, so after n pushes the total elements moved is bounded by about 2n. Spread over n operations that is constant time each, even though a single push can cost O(n).
Any reallocation invalidates all of them. Without reallocation, erase and insert invalidate iterators at or after the position. Reading through an invalid iterator is undefined behaviour.

qa.q: How do you remove all elements equal to x from a vector?
qa.a: With the erase-remove idiom: v.erase(remove(v.begin(), v.end(), x), v.end()). remove compacts the kept elements to the front in one pass and returns the new end; erase drops the tail. It is O(n) and keeps the order.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
- size is in use, capacity is allocated; growth doubles capacity.
- push_back is amortised O(1); `reserve` avoids reallocations.
- Reallocation invalidates all iterators, pointers and references.
- Erasing in an index loop skips the next element.
- Use `erase(remove(...), end())`, or `remove_if` for a condition.

quiz.stem: After `vector<int> v; v.reserve(10);` what are size() and capacity()?
quiz.explanation: reserve allocates space but creates no elements.

quiz.stem: `auto& first = v[0]; v.push_back(5);` with size() == capacity() before the push. Is `first` safe to use?
options: No: the push reallocated and first dangles
Only if v had one element
quiz.explanation: A full vector reallocates on push_back, invalidating every reference into it.

quiz.stem: What does `v.size()` return right after `remove(v.begin(), v.end(), 0)` on {0, 1, 0, 2}?
quiz.explanation: remove only reorders; size changes only after erase.

quiz.stem: Time to remove all occurrences of x from n elements with erase-remove?
quiz.explanation: One pass to compact, one erase of the tail.

hands_on.title: Remove every absent mark
hands_on.task: Read `n` and `x`, then `n` integers. Fill in `removeAll` so it removes **every** element equal to `x` and keeps the others in order. The program prints the rest, space-separated, or `empty` if nothing is left.

revision_card.front: std::vector traps: what invalidates iterators, and how to remove all x?
revision_card.back: Reallocation (push_back past capacity) invalidates everything; erase/insert invalidate at and after the position. Remove all x: v.erase(remove(v.begin(), v.end(), x), v.end()), O(n). reserve(n) allocates, resize(n) creates.
